newsitem.title: ITALY: San Paolo turns to focus on public offer.
newsitem.headline: San Paolo turns to focus on public offer.

text.p: Italy's largest bank, San Paolo di Torino, has kicked off its privatisation with the naming of core shareholders but analysts are unsure how attractive a planned public offer will be to investors.
The Italian banking sector is awash with merger and restructuring talk.
But there is little concrete evidence to tempt investors to believe good returns could be gained from this over-manned and over-bureaucratic industry, analysts said on Thursday.
The foundation that indirectly controls 65 percent of San Paolo said late on Wednesday that it would sell stakes in the bank to five shareholders in the first stage of its privatisation.

Spanish bank Banco Santander, Agnelli family holding company IFI and investment bank IMI will each take five percent stakes, while Banca Monte dei Paschi di Siena and Turin-based insurer Reale Mutua Assicurazioni will each take three percent stakes.

This was in line with earlier plans to place around 20 percent with a stable core of shareholders and then float 25 percent on the stock market by the end of June, leaving the foundation with some 20 percent.
"The big surprise is that there were no surprises. These are all close friends of San Paolo," said one Milan-based analyst.
San Paolo has left the door open for other core shareholders to come in with smaller stakes, while the pricing of the shares has yet to be decided.
Currently, Banco Santander and IMI have options to increase their stakes at 10,300 lire ($6) a share -- which compares with a current price on the bourse of around 11,800.

Analysts say San Paolo has clearly been cautious over the privatisation process, worried that the banking sector's poor performance would not attract investors, and has been keen to attract old friends into a circle of core shareholders.

An initial round of Italian bank privatisations took place in the early 1990s but many shares now languish below their placement levels, reflecting their poor returns on equity and lack of strong management keen to push through restructuring.
A 35 percent San Paolo stake was floated on the market in early 1993 at a price of 12,000 lire but four years on the shares are below that level.

Attention now focuses on the prospects for the 25 percent public placement. Analysts say San Paolo has its plus points with the largest network of retail banking outlets in Italy, the leading municiple finance operator Crediop and increasing returns from its money management.
"Within a year it has moved to first place from ninth in mutual funds managed, has good potential in insurance and is selling off unproductive assets," said another Milan analyst.
It has made great strides over the last year but other analysts await more restructuring and better management.
"It's an expensive stock with limited growth and the public placement will need to be priced at 11,000 lire or less to get the issue away," said an analyst with a British bank.
